loveLanguage.r_words_t: Your Love Language: Words of Affirmation
loveLanguage.r_words_d: For you, love is all about words. A sincere compliment, an "I love you" whispered at just the right moment, a sentence that recognizes your worth, that's what makes your heart sing. You need to hear what your partner feels, not just guess it. Words are the most tangible proof of love for you, because they require the other person to pause, reflect, and express what they truly feel. Silence, even when well-meaning, can sometimes feel cold or distant to you. A careless criticism can wound you deeply, precisely because words carry immense weight in your emotional world.
loveLanguage.r_words_a: Let your partner know that words matter to you, it's not superficial, it's simply how you receive love. Encourage little daily affirmations, messages throughout the day, even simple declarations. And in return, don't hesitate to express your own feelings with words too: your partner will learn by example.
loveLanguage.r_acts_t: Your Love Language: Acts of Service
loveLanguage.r_acts_d: For you, love is proven through actions, not speeches. When your partner takes on a task without being asked, anticipates your needs, or lifts a weight off your daily routine, that's when you truly feel loved. It's not about laziness or comfort, it's that in your view of love, to love means to act for the other person. Every concrete gesture is proof of attention and devotion. On the flip side, a partner who makes promises without following through or who lets all the responsibilities fall on your shoulders can make you feel like you don't matter.
loveLanguage.r_acts_a: Communicate clearly about what genuinely helps you, without expecting your partner to guess. Offer to exchange acts of service so the balance feels fair. And remember: if your partner has a different love language, their way of showing love might look different from what you expect. Learn to recognize those gestures too.
loveLanguage.r_gifts_d: Contrary to popular belief, this love language has nothing to do with materialism. For you, a gift is a symbol, it's proof that your partner thought of you, took the time to choose something that fits who you are. A little note slipped into your bag, a flower picked along the way, an object that recalls a shared memory, that's what truly moves you. What matters isn't the price tag, but the intention and thoughtfulness behind the gesture. A complete lack of these small tokens can leave you feeling invisible or forgotten in the relationship.
loveLanguage.r_gifts_a: Explain to your partner that it's the symbolic gestures that count, not the cost. Give them real examples of what makes you happy, what moves you. And don't hesitate to lead by example, offering small thoughtful surprises of your own. It creates a wonderful cycle of generosity and closeness in your relationship.
loveLanguage.r_time_d: For you, nothing beats time spent together. Not just being in the same room, but truly being present for each other, no phones, no distractions, with genuine and undivided attention. You need to feel that your partner actively chooses to spend time with you, that you are their priority. A walk together, a deep conversation, a shared activity, these are the moments where you feel connected and loved. On the other hand, a partner who's constantly distracted, cancels your time together, or is always glued to their phone can hurt you deeply.
loveLanguage.r_time_a: Create rituals for two that are non-negotiable: a weekly dinner date, a daily walk, a screen-free moment every evening. Explain to your partner that the quality of your time together matters just as much as the quantity. And when you're together, be fully present yourself, lead by example with the undivided attention you're looking for.
loveLanguage.r_touch_d: For you, physical contact is the most direct path to the heart. A gentle brush, a hand placed on your back, a spontaneous hug, holding hands while walking, these gestures connect you to your partner in a way that words alone can't reach. It's not just about sexuality, it's a deep need for closeness, warmth, and physical presence that reassures you and makes you feel loved. The absence of physical contact, even in a relationship that's loving in other ways, can create a sense of loneliness and emotional distance that's hard to put into words.
loveLanguage.r_touch_a: Talk openly with your partner about your need for physical touch, making clear that it goes far beyond sexual intimacy. Suggest moments of tenderness with no expectations: a morning hug, holding hands, an evening massage. If your partner is less tactile, find a rhythm together that works for both of you, without pressure, but with consistency.

vraifaux.q1: Couples who never argue are the strongest.
vraifaux.q1exp: False. Psychologist John Gottman's research shows that a total absence of conflict is often a sign that both partners are avoiding real issues. Stable couples do argue, but they know how to end their arguments.
vraifaux.q2exp: False. Jealousy is an emotional reaction rooted in insecurity, not love. A healthy attachment doesn't require monitoring or possessiveness.
vraifaux.q3: Opposites attract in a lasting way.
vraifaux.q3exp: False, or at least very nuanced. While differences can create initial attraction, studies show that couples who share core values are more stable over the long term.
vraifaux.q4: Trying new activities together strengthens the romantic bond.
vraifaux.q4exp: True. Novelty stimulates dopamine, the same circuit as early-relationship feelings. Trying something together that neither of you masters creates a particular kind of closeness.
vraifaux.q5: Romantic love can last a lifetime.
vraifaux.q5exp: True. Neuroscience studies (notably by Helen Fisher) scanned the brains of people married for over 20 years who said they were still in love. The areas associated with romantic love were still active.
vraifaux.q6: Sharing the same passions is essential for a happy couple.
vraifaux.q6exp: False. Shared interests help, but what matters more is respecting each other's passions, even those you don't share. Many very happy couples have very different interests.
vraifaux.q7: Sharing a bed improves sleep quality for both partners.
vraifaux.q7exp: False, generally. Studies show that sharing a bed disrupts sleep for most people, especially if one partner moves a lot or snores. What strengthens a couple is the quality of shared time, not necessarily the bed.
vraifaux.q8: Making love after an argument really solves the problem.
vraifaux.q8exp: False. Sex can reduce emotional tension, but without a real conversation about what caused the argument, the problem remains and comes back.
vraifaux.q9: Communication is the number one key to lasting couples.
vraifaux.q9exp: True, with a nuance: it's the quality of communication that matters, not the quantity. Talking a lot but badly can make things worse. Stable couples know how to express their needs without attacking.
vraifaux.q10: A couple can truly recover from infidelity.
vraifaux.q10exp: True. Studies on couples therapy show that around 50 to 60% of couples who choose to work through infidelity manage to rebuild a satisfying relationship. It's not automatic, but it's possible.
vraifaux.q11: Couples who live together before marriage are more likely to divorce.
vraifaux.q11exp: False, this myth has a long life. Recent studies show that cohabitation before marriage does not increase divorce rates. What matters more is the reason you move in together.
vraifaux.q12: Having children increases happiness in a couple.
vraifaux.q12exp: False, on average. Most studies show a drop in relationship satisfaction after the birth of the first child, especially in the early years. The couples who fare best are those who had time to build a solid foundation first.
vraifaux.q13: You can genuinely fall in love with someone you've never met in person.
vraifaux.q13exp: True. Studies on online relationships show that emotions linked to love, attachment, intrusive thoughts, desire, develop in the same way, with or without physical contact.
vraifaux.q14: Couples who fight hard love hard.
vraifaux.q14exp: False. The intensity of an argument is not a sign of love, it's often a sign of poor communication. The most fulfilled couples manage conflict with less drama, not more.
vraifaux.q15exp: True. Temporary distance can activate the desire and attachment system. That's why reunions after a separation are often intense. The problem is when absence becomes the only fuel for the relationship.
vraifaux.q16: Love inevitably fades over the years.
vraifaux.q16exp: False. It transforms, the intensity of early love gives way to something calmer and more stable, but that's not a decrease. Many long-term couples report a deep and lasting attachment, different but just as strong.
vraifaux.q17: Watching porn together strengthens intimacy in a couple.
vraifaux.q17exp: Nuanced but generally false. Studies are mixed: for some couples it works, for others it creates unrealistic expectations or negative comparisons. The effect depends heavily on context and communication.
vraifaux.q18: It's possible to love two people at the same time.
vraifaux.q18exp: True. Neurology confirms it: the brain can maintain simultaneous romantic attachments. This says nothing about the morality of it, but it's a documented emotional reality.
vraifaux.q19: The closer a couple is, the less they need time apart.
vraifaux.q19exp: False. The most fulfilled couples are often those who maintain an active individual life outside the relationship. Time alone or with their own friends also nourishes the couple.
vraifaux.q20: Love at first sight is a real phenomenon, not just an expression.
vraifaux.q20exp: True. Studies show that intense, sudden attraction activates many areas of the brain within seconds, dopamine, adrenaline, serotonin. It's not poetry, it's chemistry.
vraifaux.q21: Women are naturally more romantic than men.
vraifaux.q21exp: False. Studies show that men fall in love faster, are more likely to say 'I love you' first, and suffer more after a breakup. The cliché of the unromantic man doesn't match the data.
vraifaux.q22: A happy couple never has any secrets from each other.
vraifaux.q22exp: False. Having an inner life, private thoughts, or personal space is not incompatible with a healthy relationship. Total transparency is neither necessary nor always desirable.
vraifaux.q23: Friendship is a bad foundation for a romantic relationship.
vraifaux.q23exp: False, it's often the opposite. Couples who describe themselves as good friends report higher relationship satisfaction. Gottman calls it the 'friendship foundation' of stable couples.
vraifaux.q24: When you truly love someone, you never want to be anywhere else.
vraifaux.q24exp: False. Wanting solitude, space, or evenings with friends says nothing about the strength of your love. It's just a normal human need for autonomy.
vraifaux.q25: Men think about sex every seven seconds.
vraifaux.q25exp: False. This stat is an urban legend with no serious scientific basis. A study from Ohio University found that men think about sex an average of 19 times a day, already far from every 7 seconds, and not that far from women (10 times).
vraifaux.q26: A couple absolutely must share the same political views.
vraifaux.q26exp: False. Many couples with different political convictions work very well, as long as they respect each other. What causes problems is when core values (not just opinions) are incompatible.
vraifaux.q27: Watching TV series together is an activity that strengthens a couple.
vraifaux.q27exp: True, not just a joke. Research shows that sharing a common fiction (characters, stories, references) creates a sense of belonging and can even partially compensate for a limited social network.
vraifaux.q28exp: False. A well-lived routine is often synonymous with security and comfort in a relationship. What kills love is endured routine, the kind you didn't choose and never question.
vraifaux.q29: If a relationship requires effort, it means they're not the right one.
vraifaux.q29exp: False. All lasting relationships require conscious effort. The idea that 'the right one' makes everything easy is one of the most harmful romantic myths out there.
vraifaux.q30: Couples who laugh together stay together.
vraifaux.q30exp: True, to some extent. Shared humour is a predictor of relationship satisfaction in multiple studies. Laughing together indicates emotional compatibility and a similar way of seeing the world.
vraifaux.q31: A long-distance relationship is doomed to fail.
vraifaux.q31exp: False. Studies on LDRs show that their breakup rate is not significantly higher than regular relationships. What matters is having a shared vision for the future.
vraifaux.q32: Your partner's ex is always a threat.
vraifaux.q32exp: False. The vast majority of relationships with an ex stay in the past. Jealousy about exes is often more revealing of personal insecurities than any real danger.
vraifaux.q33exp: False. Making individual decisions, about your social life, money, personal projects, is healthy and necessary. A relationship where everything must be validated by the other can slide into control.
vraifaux.q34: When you're truly in love, you no longer find anyone else attractive.
vraifaux.q34exp: False. Finding someone else physically attractive is an involuntary reaction that says nothing about the strength of your feelings. Fidelity isn't the absence of attraction, it's the choice you make with it.
vraifaux.q35: Married couples are happier than unmarried couples.
vraifaux.q35exp: False, generally. Studies show that it's the quality of the relationship that predicts happiness, not legal status. Long-term unmarried couples report comparable happiness levels to married ones.
vraifaux.q36: A couple must always share the same bed.
vraifaux.q36exp: False. 'Sleep divorce', each person in their own bed or room, is gaining popularity for good reasons. Sleeping better improves mood, patience, and the quality of interactions during the day.
vraifaux.q37: Couples who post a lot on social media are the happiest.
vraifaux.q37exp: False, often the opposite. Studies have shown a correlation between excessive display of one's relationship on social media and insecurity within the relationship. The most confident people need less external validation.
vraifaux.q38: Saying 'I love you' every day loses its value.
vraifaux.q38exp: False. Repeating words of love regularly strengthens emotional security, as long as it stays sincere. What empties words of meaning is saying them on autopilot without thinking them.
vraifaux.q39: A strong couple doesn't need therapy.
vraifaux.q39exp: False. Couples therapy isn't a last-resort lifeline, it's a preventive tool. Many thriving couples do it to improve their communication before problems set in.
vraifaux.q40: Quiet arguments are less serious than loud ones.
vraifaux.q40exp: False. The volume of an argument says nothing about its severity. A cold, distant conversation can be far more damaging than an emotionally frank confrontation. What matters is the content and what follows.
vraifaux.q41: In the United States, roughly 40% of marriages end in divorce.
vraifaux.q41exp: True. According to CDC data, about 41% of first marriages in the US end in divorce. The commonly cited '50%' figure is misleading and outdated. The rate has actually been declining since its peak in the 1980s.
vraifaux.q42: The average age at first marriage in the US has remained stable since the 1970s.
vraifaux.q42exp: False. The average age at first marriage in the US has risen dramatically. In the 1970s, it was about 21 for women and 23 for men. Today it's approximately 29 for women and 30 for men, a shift of nearly a decade in two generations.
vraifaux.q43: More than one in four couples in the US met online.
vraifaux.q43exp: True. According to The Knot's 2025 study, about 27% of couples who married in 2025 met through a dating app. Other studies put the figure even higher for all new couples, including unmarried ones.
vraifaux.q44: Couples who make love at least once a week are significantly happier than others.
vraifaux.q44exp: True, with a nuance. Studies show that going from zero to once a week significantly improves reported happiness in a couple. Beyond once a week, the plateau effect kicks in and frequency adds little more.
vraifaux.q45: Valentine's Day is the most commercialised holiday of the year in the United States.
vraifaux.q45exp: False. Christmas remains by far the most commercialised holiday in the US, followed by Back-to-School season. Valentine's Day spending is significant but comes well behind.
vraifaux.q46: Childless couples are on average more satisfied with their relationship.
vraifaux.q46exp: True, statistically. Studies consistently show that relationship satisfaction drops after the birth of a child, especially in the early years. That doesn't mean children make people unhappy, but the impact on the couple is real.
vraifaux.q47: The average length of a marriage before divorce in the US is under 10 years.
vraifaux.q47exp: True. In the US, first marriages last an average of 8 to 9 years before ending in divorce. This is shorter than in most European countries, where the average is closer to 15 years.
vraifaux.q48: Men suffer as much as women after a breakup.
vraifaux.q48exp: True, or even more in some ways. Studies show that men suffer longer after a breakup, even if they show it less. Women tend to suffer more intensely at first but recover faster.
vraifaux.q49: Common-law marriages are recognised in all 50 US states.
vraifaux.q49exp: False. Only a handful of US states still recognise common-law marriages, including Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, and Texas. Most states require a formal marriage licence and ceremony.
vraifaux.q50: Couples who share household chores equally have sex more often.
vraifaux.q50exp: True. Studies (notably from Cornell University) show that perceived fairness in domestic tasks is correlated with better sexual satisfaction and higher frequency.
vraifaux.q51: Nearly 30% of all households in the United States are occupied by a single person.
vraifaux.q51exp: True. About 29% of US households are single-person households, a figure that has nearly doubled since the 1960s. The trend is driven by later marriage, higher divorce rates, and longer lifespans.
vraifaux.q52: Couples who travel together at least once a year are happier.
vraifaux.q52exp: True according to several studies on relationship happiness. Shared experiences outside of daily life, including travel, are among the most effective investments in relationship satisfaction.
vraifaux.q53: The majority of divorces in the United States are initiated by women.
vraifaux.q53exp: True. Studies show that about 69% of divorces in the US are initiated by women. Among college-educated women, the figure is even higher at about 90%. The most cited reasons: unmet needs and infidelity.
vraifaux.q54: Fewer than 10% of arranged marriages end in divorce.
vraifaux.q54exp: False, the numbers vary enormously by country and culture. Some studies cite very low divorce rates in arranged marriages, but this is often conflated with contexts where divorce is socially or legally difficult.
vraifaux.q55: Couples who eat together regularly are closer.
vraifaux.q55exp: True. Shared meals are one of the most documented couple rituals in relational psychology. Eating together without screens creates a regular space for connection that strengthens attachment.
vraifaux.q56: In the United States, infidelity is more common among men than women.
vraifaux.q56exp: True according to available studies. Surveys show that about 20-25% of American men report having cheated, compared to 10-15% of women. The gap narrows among younger generations.
vraifaux.q57: Long-distance couples communicate more on average than couples who live together.
vraifaux.q57exp: True. By necessity, long-distance couples have more intentional and often deeper exchanges. Several studies note they share more personal and emotional information than couples who see each other every day.
vraifaux.q58: The number of marriages in the United States increases every year.
vraifaux.q58exp: False. The US marriage rate has been declining for decades. While there were brief upticks (notably after COVID postponements), the long-term trend shows a steady decline from 10.6 marriages per 1,000 people in 1970 to about 6.0 today.
vraifaux.q59: Happy couples give each other roughly five compliments for every criticism.
vraifaux.q59exp: True, this is what John Gottman calls the 'magic ratio' (5:1). In stable couples, positive interactions outnumber negative ones by about 5 to 1. Below 1 to 1, the relationship is in danger.
vraifaux.q60: The majority of American adults live with a partner.
vraifaux.q60exp: True. About 53-55% of American adults live with a spouse or partner, though this figure has been declining. In 1990, about 65% of adults were part of a couple.
vraifaux.q61: Giving flowers for no reason is more appreciated than giving them for an anniversary.
vraifaux.q61exp: True according to several studies on acts of kindness. An unexpected gift, with no particular occasion, is perceived as more sincere than an expected one. The surprise effect matters a lot.
vraifaux.q62: Checking your phone during a meal with your partner is considered acceptable by most couples.
vraifaux.q62exp: False. The vast majority of people in relationships describe phones at the table as a major source of irritation. The term 'phubbing' (ignoring someone in favour of your phone) is associated with lower relationship satisfaction.
vraifaux.q63: Couples who cook together are generally more satisfied with their relationship.
vraifaux.q63exp: True. Cooking together combines coordination, creativity, and sharing, it's a natural ground for closeness. Studies on relationship wellbeing cite collaborative home activities as a factor in satisfaction.
vraifaux.q64: Going to bed angry is always a bad idea.
vraifaux.q64exp: False. Contrary to popular wisdom, studies show that sleeping after a conflict can help regulate emotions and allow sensitive topics to be approached more calmly the next day.
vraifaux.q65: Couples who regularly say thank you and apologise are more stable.
vraifaux.q65exp: True. These small gestures of recognition and repair signal to the other person that they're respected. Gottman's research puts a lot of emphasis on these 'small repairs' as a pillar of stability.
vraifaux.q66: Money is the number one cause of arguments in couples.
vraifaux.q66exp: True in many studies. Money regularly tops other subjects (household chores, sex, in-laws) as a source of conflict in couples, especially when incomes are unequal or financial values differ.
vraifaux.q67: Couples who exercise together are physically closer.
vraifaux.q67exp: True. Physical activity together produces adrenaline and dopamine, two hormones that reinforce attachment. And shared effort naturally creates closeness.
vraifaux.q68: Having mutual friends is essential for a happy couple.
vraifaux.q68exp: False. Mutual friends are great, but not essential. What matters more is that each person has their own friends, and that the couple leaves room for that individual social life.
vraifaux.q69: Short separations (weekends or weeks apart) can be good for a couple.
vraifaux.q69exp: True. A little voluntary distance can renew desire and remind each person what they appreciate about the other. Many couples therapists recommend it when routine has set in too deeply.
vraifaux.q70: You must share a joint bank account for a relationship to work.
vraifaux.q70exp: False. Financial management in a couple (joint account, separate accounts, or both) is not an indicator of relationship strength. What matters is being aligned on priorities, not the mechanism chosen.
vraifaux.q71: Relationship anniversaries (of meeting, of marriage...) are important to most couples.
vraifaux.q71exp: True. Commemorative rituals are a strong marker of couple identity. Celebrating them signals to the other person that the relationship matters and that its history has value.
vraifaux.q72: Sleeping with a pet in the bedroom is bad for a couple's relationship.
vraifaux.q72exp: False. Studies on this topic show very mixed results. For the majority of couples with a pet, its presence in the bedroom doesn't disrupt the relationship, and for many, it even reinforces the sense of comfort.
vraifaux.q73: Giving gifts is the best way to express love.
vraifaux.q73exp: False. According to Gary Chapman's '5 Love Languages' concept, each person has a preferred mode of expression: gifts, quality time, physical touch, words of affirmation, or acts of service. What matters is speaking the other person's language, not your own.
vraifaux.q74: Couples who talk about their relationship with friends are more stable.
vraifaux.q74exp: Nuanced. Having social support is useful, but sharing the details of your conflicts with your circle can create problematic loyalties and outside judgements that complicate reconciliation.
vraifaux.q75: Looking at old photos together strengthens romantic feelings.
vraifaux.q75exp: True. Shared nostalgia activates positive emotions and reinforces the sense of belonging to a common history. It's one of the simplest and most effective couple rituals.
vraifaux.q76: Couples who share the same TV series have fewer conflicts.
vraifaux.q76exp: False, no established link to conflict. However, watching series together creates shared references and moments of connection that reinforce closeness.
vraifaux.q77: It's normal to sometimes feel bored in a relationship.
vraifaux.q77exp: True. Boredom is a normal emotion in any long relationship. What distinguishes lasting couples is that they treat boredom as a signal (time to invent something together) rather than a verdict (this isn't working anymore).
vraifaux.q78: Couples who eat in bed are less satisfied with their intimate life.
vraifaux.q78exp: False, no serious study supports this. Eating in bed together is even often associated with a relaxed, informal intimacy that many couples enjoy.
vraifaux.q79: Spending more time together always improves the quality of a relationship.
vraifaux.q79exp: False. Beyond a certain threshold, more time together can increase friction and reduce satisfaction. The quality of shared time matters far more than the quantity.
vraifaux.q80: Couples who plan their dates are more fulfilled than those who improvise.
vraifaux.q80exp: True according to several studies. Planning time together (even ordinary moments) shows that the relationship is a conscious priority. Improvisation alone tends to leave couple life on the margins of daily routine.
vraifaux.q81: Romeo and Juliet in Shakespeare had known each other for less than a week when they married.
vraifaux.q81exp: True. In the play, they meet on a Sunday evening and marry the following Monday. It's one of the most famous love stories in the world, and also one of the most rushed.
vraifaux.q82: Beyoncé and Jay-Z have been together for over 20 years.
vraifaux.q82exp: True. They've been together since 2001 and married in 2008. Despite publicly acknowledged crises (Beyoncé's Lemonade album in 2016), they're still together.
vraifaux.q83: Brad Pitt and Jennifer Aniston met on a film set.
vraifaux.q83exp: False. They met through their respective managers, at a private party. They never appeared in a film together.
vraifaux.q84: James Cameron's Titanic is based on a real love story.
vraifaux.q84exp: False. The characters Jack and Rose are fictional. The film is inspired by the real sinking of the Titanic in 1912, but the central couple is entirely invented.
vraifaux.q85: Marie Curie and Pierre Curie won the Nobel Prize together.
vraifaux.q85exp: True. They shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, with Henri Becquerel. Marie Curie is the only person to have received two Nobel Prizes in two different disciplines.
vraifaux.q86: Marilyn Monroe sang 'Happy Birthday' to President Kennedy as his confirmed romantic partner.
vraifaux.q86exp: False. While Marilyn Monroe's breathy 'Happy Birthday, Mr. President' performance in 1962 is one of the most iconic moments in American pop culture, no romantic relationship between Monroe and JFK has ever been officially confirmed. It remains one of the most persistent unproven celebrity rumours in history.
vraifaux.q87: Victoria and David Beckham have been together since the 1990s.
vraifaux.q87exp: True. They met in 1997 and married in 1999. Their relationship has lasted over 25 years, making them one of the most enduring couples in show business.
vraifaux.q88exp: True. 'Flirter' comes from the old French 'fleureter', meaning to talk about flowers, and by extension to say nice things to someone. English borrowed it and handed it back to us in a slightly different form.
vraifaux.q89exp: True, in part. Saint Valentine is a Christian martyr from the 3rd century. But the association with romantic love came much later, in the Middle Ages, notably through Chaucer's writings.
vraifaux.q90: The term 'honeymoon' comes from a tradition of drinking mead for a month after the wedding.
vraifaux.q90exp: True. In some Nordic and Germanic cultures, newlyweds consumed mead (a honey-based drink) for a 'moon' (one month) after the wedding. Hence 'honeymoon'.
vraifaux.q91: The tradition that an engagement ring should cost three months' salary is centuries old.
vraifaux.q91exp: False. The 'three months' salary' rule was invented by De Beers' marketing campaigns in the 1980s. Before that, they had promoted one month's salary, and before that, two months'. There is no genuine tradition behind it, just brilliant advertising.
vraifaux.q92: Shakira and Gerard Piqué were together for more than 10 years.
vraifaux.q92exp: True. They met at the 2010 World Cup and were together from 2011 to 2022, 11 years and two children.
vraifaux.q93: The world record for the longest marriage is over 80 years.
vraifaux.q93exp: True. Several couples have surpassed 80 years of marriage, with documented records around 86 years. These cases are extremely rare but real.
vraifaux.q94: Engagement rings have always existed in their current form.
vraifaux.q94exp: False. The diamond engagement ring tradition is relatively recent, popularised in the 1930s and 40s by a De Beers marketing campaign with the slogan 'A Diamond is Forever'. Before that, engagement rings existed, but a diamond was far from the norm.
vraifaux.q95: The first couple shown in the same bed on American television appeared in 'The Brady Bunch'.
vraifaux.q95exp: False. It was 'The Mary Kay and Johnny Show' in 1947, a little-known but pioneering show. 'The Brady Bunch' (1969) came much later.
vraifaux.q96: In the United States, you can legally marry a deceased person.
vraifaux.q96exp: False. Unlike France, where posthumous marriage is legally possible with presidential authorisation, no US state allows marriage to a deceased person. Some states allow proxy marriages for military personnel, but both parties must be alive when the process begins.
vraifaux.q97: The average cost of a wedding in the United States exceeds $30,000.
vraifaux.q97exp: True. According to The Knot, the average cost of a US wedding in 2024 was about $33,000. However, the median is much lower at around $13,000, meaning a small number of very expensive weddings heavily skew the average.
vraifaux.q98: The word 'marriage' comes from the Latin 'matrimonium'.
vraifaux.q98exp: True. 'Matrimonium' itself comes from 'mater' (mother), which tells us something about what marriage originally signified: an institution centred on motherhood and transmission.
vraifaux.q99: In the United States, it is legal to marry your first cousin in every state.

pervers.r1_d: Based on your answers, your relationship doesn't show the markers of narcissistic abuse. Like every couple you have disagreements and clumsy moments, but your partner respects your word, your limits and your freedom. Emotional safety seems to be there.

pervers.r2_t: A few signals to keep an eye on
pervers.r2_d: Some of your answers point to behaviours that deserve your attention: occasional put-downs, difficulty owning mistakes, or moments when you feel on the defensive. This doesn't necessarily make your partner a narcissist, but these dynamics can take root if nothing is named.
pervers.r2_a: Dare to set a clear limit and watch the reaction: a respectful partner adjusts, a manipulator escalates. Keep a factual journal of what hurts you to see things more clearly, and talk to someone you trust.
pervers.r3_d: Several of your answers describe mechanisms typical of coercive control: gaslighting, reversed guilt, isolation, the idealise / devalue cycle. You may be walking on eggshells and doubting your own perception. Repeated, these patterns deeply damage self-esteem.
pervers.r3_a: This result deserves to be taken seriously. Reconnect with reality by keeping a journal of the facts, break the isolation and, ideally, get support from a professional (a psychologist or a specialised organisation). You are not responsible for the other person's behaviour.
pervers.r4_t: A profile strongly suggestive of a narcissist
pervers.r4_d: Your answers paint a worrying picture, very close to the mechanics of narcissistic abuse: manipulation, lack of empathy, control, blackmail and the gradual destruction of your self-confidence. This kind of relationship is exhausting and can endanger your mental, sometimes physical, health.
pervers.r4_a: Don't carry this weight alone. Reach out to a professional and to organisations that support victims of psychological abuse. In case of immediate danger, contact the emergency services. This test is not a diagnosis, but it confirms one thing: you have every right to protect yourself.

habitude.r1_t: A love that's very much alive
habitude.r1_d: Your answers breathe love far more than habit. The early passion may have evolved, but it has given way to a deep attachment, a real desire to share and to choose the other. Your relationship is a source of joy, not just a routine.
habitude.r1_a: Keep nurturing this precious bond: the little gestures, the plans, the moments of closeness and desire. A living love is cultivated every day, and that's clearly what you're already doing.
habitude.r2_t: Love wins, but routine is settling in
habitude.r2_d: The love is there, but routine is starting to nibble at your relationship. That's perfectly normal after a few years: daily life takes over and the little attentions space out. Nothing alarming, but a signal not to let habit smother what you truly feel.
habitude.r2_a: Rekindle the spark on purpose: surprises, one-on-one time, new experiences together. Talk again about your wishes and dreams. Often, simply putting the relationship back at the top of your priorities brings the spark back.
habitude.r3_d: Your answers show that habit now takes up more room than the pull of love. You probably still care about your partner, but the desire, the closeness and the urge to plan ahead have faded. It's not a foregone conclusion, but it calls for real awareness.
habitude.r3_a: Ask yourself honestly: do I want to revive this relationship, or is it mainly fear of change that holds me? If you want to believe in it, working on it together (honest dialogue, couples therapy) can restart the engine. The worst would be to drift without deciding anything.
habitude.r4_t: It's mostly habit that binds you
habitude.r4_d: Based on your answers, it's habit, comfort or fear that hold you far more than love. Desire, closeness and the wish for a shared future seem to have gone out. It doesn't mean all is lost, but the current status quo probably isn't making you happy.
habitude.r4_a: Give yourself real time to reflect, alone and then together. Do you want to try to rebuild something alive, or have you drifted apart for good? There's no shame in asking the question, and support (a psychologist, a couples therapist) can help you see clearly.

tentation.r1_t: Unshakeable: the island had no hold on you
tentation.r1_d: Twelve days of paradise beaches, stunning singles and staged temptations, and you didn't move an inch. You set your limits on day one and stuck to them without even having to think about it. On the island, couples like yours come home stronger than they arrived.
tentation.r1_a: Your strength isn't willpower, it's clarity. You know what you want and you aren't starving for anything. Keep feeding that bond: it's exactly what made you immune.
tentation.r2_d: You felt things, a look, a compliment, a moment of drift, and that is perfectly human. But every time the line got close, you stepped back. You'd come home from the island with a clear conscience and maybe one or two awkward moments at the bonfire, nothing more.
tentation.r2_a: Being tempted isn't betrayal: what counts is acting on it, and you didn't. Still, note what unsettled you: it's often the sign of a need going unmet at home.
tentation.r3_t: In danger: the line got blurry
tentation.r3_d: The island did its job. Between the overly intimate confidences, the ambiguous moments and the closeness you didn't really prevent, your partner would have plenty to hurt over watching the footage. You may not have done anything irreparable, but you didn't stop anything either.
tentation.r3_a: This result isn't a conviction, it's a signal. Ask yourself honestly what you were looking for on that island: attention, desire, lightness? That same need exists in your real life, and that's where it has to be addressed.
tentation.r4_t: The bonfire is going to hurt
tentation.r4_d: You gave in, several times, and not just half-heartedly. On the island, your behaviour looks a lot more like a single person's than someone in a relationship. The final bonfire is going to be brutal: the footage speaks for itself.
tentation.r4_a: The real question isn't “did I resist?” but “why didn't I want to resist?”. An affair never creates a crack, it reveals one that was already there. It's time to look at that crack together.
tentation.r5_t: You're leaving alone (or with someone else)
tentation.r5_d: There was no suspense. From the first days you were already elsewhere, and the island only confirmed what you probably knew before you left. Temptation didn't break your relationship: it simply sped up a story that was already over.

attachement.pf_secure_d: You have a secure attachment: you're comfortable with both intimacy and independence. You express your needs clearly, you trust your partner, and conflict doesn't threaten the bond you share.
attachement.pf_secure_a: Your emotional security is a real strength for your relationship. You can be a stabilising anchor for a partner with a more anxious or avoidant style, as long as you don't take on the whole emotional load by yourself.
attachement.pf_anxious_d: Your attachment leans anxious: you have an intense need for closeness and reassurance. The fear of abandonment can push you to over-analyse your partner's behaviour, to seek constant proof of love, and to feel destabilised by the smallest distance.
attachement.pf_anxious_a: Learn to self-soothe when the anxiety rises: breathing, grounding, writing down what you feel before reacting. And name your need for reassurance out loud rather than testing your partner, a request is always heard better than a test.
attachement.pf_avoidant_d: Your attachment leans avoidant: you value your independence highly. Emotional intimacy can feel intrusive, and your instinct when things get intense is to create distance, often without meaning to hurt anyone.
attachement.pf_avoidant_a: Practise staying present in moments of intimacy rather than pulling away automatically. And when you need space, say so instead of taking it silently: a stated need protects the bond, a silent withdrawal damages it.
attachement.pf_disorganized_d: Your attachment combines anxious and avoidant traits: you swing between a strong desire for connection and a fear of intimacy. You may draw closer then push away, which is exhausting for you and confusing for your partner.
attachement.pf_disorganized_a: This profile benefits particularly from support: therapy helps make sense of these contradictory movements, which usually have their roots well before your current relationship. In the meantime, naming the swing out loud already takes a lot of pressure off your partner.

confiance.r2_a: Talk openly about these grey areas with your partner. Unspoken things usually feed mistrust more than reality does. Set up regular communication rituals to defuse tension before it settles in.

confiance.r3_d: Overall, you trust your partner and they trust you. A few points of vigilance remain, but nothing worrying. Your relationship rests on healthy foundations.
confiance.r3_a: Keep cultivating transparency and communication. Small daily gestures (keeping your promises, being reliable) strengthen trust day after day. You're on the right track!
confiance.r4_d: Well done! Your relationship rests on solid, reciprocal trust. You feel emotionally safe, free to be yourself and able to count on each other without anxiety.
confiance.r4_a: This trust is a treasure, don't take it for granted. Keep being transparent, keep your commitments and welcome your partner's vulnerability. That's what makes the good stories last.

infidelite.q16c: Several inconsistencies in their stories, piling up over time.
infidelite.q16d: Blatant lies about their activities, who they see or their schedule.
infidelite.q17: How does your partner react when you voice worries about your relationship?
infidelite.q17a: They listen, reassure me and we discuss it calmly.
infidelite.q17b: They listen but seem a little uncomfortable with the subject.
infidelite.q17c: They play down what I feel or tell me I'm imagining things.
infidelite.q17d: They accuse me of being jealous or controlling, and turn it around to make me feel guilty.
infidelite.q18: Has your partner changed their habits around going out?
infidelite.q18a: No, I broadly know where they go and it's transparent.
infidelite.q18b: A few unplanned outings, but they let me know.
infidelite.q18c: They leave without warning, give vague explanations or change their story.
infidelite.q18d: They're regularly away with no valid reason and react badly if I ask where they were.
infidelite.q19: Do you feel a diffuse tension or unease you can't explain?
infidelite.q19a: No, I feel safe and settled in my relationship.
infidelite.q19b: A slight doubt sometimes, which passes quickly.
infidelite.q19c: Yes, something tells me things aren't right, without my being able to pin it down.
infidelite.q19d: My gut is screaming that something is going on, and the anxiety has become daily.
infidelite.q20: Overall, how would you rate the transparency in your relationship right now?
infidelite.q20a: Excellent, we tell each other almost everything, in a climate of trust.
infidelite.q20b: Fine, even if there are grey areas I don't go into.
infidelite.q20c: Fragile, I feel things are slipping past me and that my partner filters what they tell me.
infidelite.q20d: Almost non-existent, I feel a wall between us and getting honest answers has become a battle.
infidelite.r1_d: Based on your answers, your relationship shows no worrying signs related to infidelity. Communication seems open, transparency is there and your partner isn't showing suspicious behaviour. Your relationship rests on solid foundations of trust.
infidelite.r1_a: Keep cultivating that trust day to day. Small gestures of transparency, open conversations and mutual respect are the best defences against the erosion of the bond. If a doubt ever comes up, raise it directly rather than letting anxiety settle in.
infidelite.r2_t: A few grey areas to keep an eye on
infidelite.r2_d: Some of your answers reveal subtle changes that deserve your attention. This isn't a diagnosis, but weak signals are present: slight distance, small inconsistencies or shifts in behaviour. These can have perfectly ordinary explanations (work stress, tiredness, personal change).
infidelite.r2_a: Before drawing conclusions, open a dialogue with your partner. Say what you feel without accusing: "I've noticed that... and it worries me a little." Most of the time, an honest conversation is enough to clear the doubts. If the situation persists, our trust test for couples can help you take your thinking further.
infidelite.r3_d: Several of your answers point to significant behavioural changes in your partner: emotional distance, secrecy around the phone, shifts in habits, defensive reactions. Taken one by one, each of these can be explained, but their accumulation is a serious signal.
infidelite.r3_a: It's time for a real conversation, not an interrogation, but a sincere exchange about the state of your relationship. Choose a calm moment and express what you feel using "I" ("I feel distant", "I need to understand"). If your partner refuses to talk or denies everything outright, consider professional support (couples therapy) to get out of the deadlock.
infidelite.r4_d: Your answers paint a worrying picture. Many indicators converge: secrecy, distance, lies, drastic changes in behaviour and defensive reactions to your questions. This result doesn't prove infidelity, but it reveals a deep imbalance in your relationship that can't go unanswered.
infidelite.r4_a: What you feel is legitimate, don't let anyone make you doubt your own perception. The next step isn't to play detective, but to lay things out clearly: say what you observe, what you feel and what you need. If dialogue is impossible, see a professional on your own to begin with, so you're supported. Your emotional wellbeing comes first.

bebe.q1: When you picture your life with a baby, your first reaction is…
bebe.q1a: A mix of excitement and calm, you feel ready to welcome that change.
bebe.q1b: Curiosity and desire, even if a few uncertainties remain.
bebe.q1c: Slight apprehension, you like the idea but it still feels abstract.
bebe.q1d: Anxiety or a mental block, you can't picture yourself in that role.

bebe.q2a: You have solid savings, a stable income and you've already worked out what a baby costs.
bebe.q2b: Your situation is decent, you could adapt by reorganising some spending.
bebe.q2c: It's a bit tight, you'd need to shore up your finances before seriously considering it.
bebe.q2d: You're in a precarious financial situation and a child would add considerable stress.

bebe.q3a: Solid, stable and fulfilling, you communicate well and get through hard times together.
bebe.q3b: Broadly good, with a few things to improve but nothing worrying.
bebe.q3c: Still being built or fragile on some points, communication could be better.
bebe.q3d: Unstable or non-existent, this isn't the right context to consider a baby.

bebe.q4a: Yes, you know it will be hard and you feel able to handle that tiredness.
bebe.q4b: You know it'll be tough but you think you can organise yourself to cope.
bebe.q4c: The idea of broken nights scares you a little, sleep matters a lot to you.
bebe.q4d: Not at all, you already struggle to function on little sleep.
bebe.q5: Do you have a support network (family, close friends) you could count on?
bebe.q5a: Yes, you have people nearby who are available and ready to help in practical ways.
bebe.q5b: You have a few trusted people, even if they're not all close by.
bebe.q5c: Your network is limited, you'd mostly have to rely on yourself.
bebe.q5d: You feel fairly isolated, there's no one you can really lean on.

bebe.q6b: You've thought about it without planning everything, but you know you'll find solutions.
bebe.q6c: It worries you, your work situation is still fragile or in transition.
bebe.q6d: You haven't thought about it at all, or your career is your absolute priority right now.
bebe.q7: How have you felt about your mental health these past few months?
bebe.q7a: Stable and settled, you handle your stress and emotions well day to day.
bebe.q7b: Pretty good, with normal ups and downs you know how to manage.
bebe.q7c: Fragile at times, you're going through a somewhat complicated period.
bebe.q7d: Difficult, you're dealing with anxiety, depression or significant burnout.
bebe.q8: Are you and your partner aligned on wanting a child?

bebe.q8b: Broadly, even if the timing or some details still need discussing.
bebe.q8c: Not really, one of you is more enthusiastic than the other.
bebe.q8d: No, there's a clear disagreement or the subject has never come up.
bebe.q9a: You have suitable space, with a room available for a child.
bebe.q9b: Your current home could work for a while, even if moving would be ideal.
bebe.q9c: Your home is small or poorly suited, a change would be needed before a baby arrives.
bebe.q9d: Your housing situation is unstable or very precarious.
bebe.q10: Can you stay patient in stressful everyday situations?
bebe.q10a: Yes, you're fairly calm and patient, even under pressure.
bebe.q10b: Most of the time, though you have your limits like everyone.
bebe.q10c: You lose your temper quite easily and you know patience isn't your strong suit.
bebe.q10d: You often feel overwhelmed by stress, even over minor things.

bebe.q11a: You stay calm and naturally try to work out what's wrong.
bebe.q11b: It affects you, you do your best to help even when it isn't easy.
bebe.q11c: It makes you uncomfortable or stresses you out quickly.
bebe.q11d: It's completely beyond you, you'd rather move away.
bebe.q12: Are you ready to put some hobbies or passions on hold for the first few years?
bebe.q12a: Yes, you know it's temporary and you accept it calmly.
bebe.q12b: You're ready to adjust your pace, even if it takes some effort.
bebe.q12c: That sacrifice weighs on you just thinking about it.
bebe.q12d: No, your personal activities are essential to your balance and you don't want to give them up.

bebe.q13b: You've thought about it and you know it matters, but nothing is settled yet.
bebe.q13c: Vaguely, you assume it'll sort itself out along the way.
bebe.q13d: Not at all, you have no idea what it involves in practice.

bebe.q14a: You adapt easily, surprises don't throw you.
bebe.q14b: You cope fine, though you prefer things planned.
bebe.q14c: Unexpected events stress you a lot and disrupt your daily life.
bebe.q14d: You need to control everything, the slightest change puts you in a difficult state.

bebe.q15b: You think so, even if you know there are still things to work on.
bebe.q15c: You're not sure, you're still figuring yourself out in some areas.
bebe.q15d: No, you feel you still have a long way to go before being ready.
bebe.q16: What's your main motivation for having a child?

bebe.q16b: The desire is growing naturally, you feel you're in a good phase of life for it.
bebe.q16c: Social or family pressure plays a part, even if there's some genuine desire.
bebe.q16d: You don't have a clear motivation, or you hope a baby would fill a void.

bebe.q17b: A few times, and you did pretty well.
bebe.q17c: Very rarely, you don't have much experience with very young children.
bebe.q17d: Never, you have no idea what daily life with a baby looks like.

bebe.q18a: You've made peace with your past and you know what kind of parent you want to be, regardless of your models.
bebe.q18b: You've gained perspective, you want to repeat some things and avoid others.
bebe.q18c: It's a sensitive subject, some wounds haven't healed yet.
bebe.q18d: Your childhood was hard and you're afraid of repeating the same patterns.
bebe.q19: Are you ready to ask for help if you need it (doctor, therapist, people around you)?
bebe.q19a: Absolutely, you know asking for help is a strength, not a weakness.
bebe.q19b: You think so, even if it isn't always easy for you.
bebe.q19c: You'd struggle, you generally prefer to manage on your own.
bebe.q19d: No, asking for help feels impossible or shameful to you.
bebe.q20: If you had to sum up how you feel about having a baby now…
bebe.q20a: You feel confident and enthusiastic, the conditions are there to go for it.
bebe.q20b: You're fairly positive, a few details remain but the essentials are in place.
bebe.q20c: You're hesitating, some important things aren't in place yet.
bebe.q20d: You feel it isn't the right time, and it's okay to acknowledge that.
bebe.r1_d: Based on your answers, several important parts of your life aren't yet aligned for welcoming a baby. Whether emotionally, financially, relationally or personally, there are fragile areas. This is neither a failure nor a judgement: it's simply a snapshot of where you are right now.
bebe.r1_a: Not being ready today doesn't mean never being ready. Take the time to shore up what needs it, whether that's your financial stability, your mental health or your relationship. The time you give yourself is a gift to your future child.
bebe.r2_d: You're not fully ready yet, but the desire is starting to take form. Some areas of your life are solid, others still need work. This is a normal and healthy phase: you're thinking it through seriously rather than rushing in.
bebe.r2_a: Identify the two or three things holding you back most and focus on those. Talk openly about your doubts with your partner, or with someone you trust. The goal isn't to reach perfection, but to feel solid enough to take the leap.
bebe.r3_d: Most of the lights are green. You've clearly thought this through, your life is fairly stable and your desire seems genuine. A few minor adjustments remain, but nothing that should hold you back for long.
bebe.r3_a: The last details to sort out (housing, organisation, conversations with your partner) can be worked on over the coming weeks or months. Don't wait for everything to be perfect, perfection doesn't exist in parenting. Trust your ability to adapt.
bebe.r4_d: Your answers show real maturity and solid preparation. Emotional, financial and relational stability: the foundations are there. Your desire seems considered, sincere and shared. That's an excellent signal.
bebe.r4_a: If the desire is there and the conditions allow it, there's no reason to wait indefinitely. The perfect moment doesn't exist, but a good moment is recognisable. Make the most of that energy and keep talking with your partner so you move forward together.
